documentation.population:
The global, native population size is rather poorly known. In Europe, the wild population is estimated at only 4,800-8,200 pairs (BirdLife International 2021). Subspecies talischensis is considered very rare and may number only 200-300 individuals (del Hoyo et al. 1994). Globally, it has been crudely estimated to be ‘possibly tens of millions’ (Giudice and Ratti 2020). This is probably accurate: densities in China have been estimated at 64-95 birds/km2 (Wang Nan et al. 2004) and it is consistently described as common; densities are much lower (1-2 birds/km2) in Mongolia (Gombobaatar et al. 2012) where, however, it is at the very limits of its range. In its mapped native range, excluding that covered by BirdLife International [2021]), there is c.4,000,000 km2 of suitable habitat (Jung et al. 2020), such that even if only 30-60% is occupied, at the densities noted the population likely numbers in the high tens of millions. The native population size is therefore placed in the band 50,000,000-100,000,000 birds. The percentage of these that are mature/breeding is unknown.

In Europe, 3,160,000-4,280,000 pairs of non-native birds are estimated (BirdLife International 2021). Other data have reported 2,300,000 breeding females In the United Kingdom alone, where numbers are supplemented by more than an order of magnitude each year for shooting: >40,000,000 pheasants are estimated to be released each year (Blackburn & Gaston 2021). The (non-native) population in the United States is estimated at 17,000,000 birds (Partners in Flight 2021). The (non-native) population in New Zealand is estimated at 250,000 birds (Seabrook-Davison 2013 [2017]). There are also non-native populations in Japan and Australia but these are not thought to add substantially to the global total. The global non-native population is therefore estimated to be 25,000,000-50,000,000 birds.
documentation.habitats: The following information refers to the species' habitat use in its European range. In its natural range, this species shows a considerable variation in its habitat. It is found chiefly in the overgrown edges of rivers, hilly areas close to cultivation and flat land which is under cultivation. In Azerbaijan, egg-laying occurs in April and May. The nest is a shallow depression in the ground, which is lined with plant material from the vicinity of the nest, or unlined. Clutches are nine to fourteen eggs. In its natural range, the species feeds on plant matter such as fruits, seeds, leaves, buds and a small amount of animal matter, for example insects. Where it is introduced it is an opportunistic omnivore, feeding on a diverse range of food, preferring large, energy rich items such as cultivated grains, mast and fruits. Mass migrations may occur in its native range but in its introduced range it is sedentary (McGowan et al. 2013).
documentation.threats: In its introduced range in Europe it is very common and wild populations are often augmented by large numbers of captive bred birds for shooting. However in Azerbaijan race talischensis has been brought to the brink of extinction due to habitat loss and uncontrolled hunting (McGowan et al. 2013) and there is no reliable information on its current status (Braasch et al. 2011).
documentation.measures:
Conservation Actions Underway
EU Birds Directive Annex II and III. There are currently no known conservation measures for this species in Europe.

Conservation Actions Proposed
In Europe, research and monitoring is needed to determine the status of race talischensis and inform future conservation measures.
documentation.use_trade: This species has been reported as used in trade at a high prevalence, being found in three of the seven trade datasets evaluated (Donald et al. 2024).
documentation.rationale: This species has an extremely large range, and hence does not approach the thresholds for Vulnerable under the range size criterion (extent of occurrence under 20,000 km² combined with a declining or fluctuating range size, habitat extent/quality, or population size and a small number of locations or severe fragmentation). The population size has not been quantified, but it is not believed to approach the thresholds for Vulnerable under the population size criterion (under 10,000 mature individuals with a continuing decline estimated to be over 10% in ten years or three generations, or with a specified population structure). The population trend is not known, but the population is not believed to be decreasing sufficiently rapidly to approach the thresholds under the population trend criterion (over 30% decline over ten years or three generations). For these reasons the species is evaluated as Least Concern.
documentation.trend_justification: The population is widespread and very common in much of its range, however populations are declining locally owing to habitat loss and over-hunting. In Europe the population is estimated to be increasing (BirdLife International 2015).
documentation.taxonomic_notes: Phasianus colchicus and P. versicolor (del Hoyo and Collar 2014) were previously lumped as P. colchicus following Sibley and Monroe (1990, 1993).
